title: Final two shots were fatal in frenzied chase, inquest hears
article: Victoria police fired a total of 12 rounds at suspected car thief John Seguin, but the last two shots likely killed the 37-year-old Victoria man, the case's lead forensic investigator said yesterday.

Testifying at a B.C. coroner's inquest into the Feb. 3, 2007, incident, Sergeant Mike Yeager described the chaos that ensued when Mr. Seguin tried to evade a police roadblock by driving down a narrow boulevard near the intersection of Hillside Avenue and Blackwood Street.
Sgt. John Ayers, who was directly in the path of the vehicle, fired three shots as the stolen GMC Jimmy Mr. Seguin was driving accelerated toward him.
Sgt. Mike Johnston, a few feet away, fired another two rounds as the vehicle sped past.

Badly damaged from a series of collisions with police cruisers before the chase, the Jimmy then careened onto Hillside Avenue, veering to the left as Constable Cliff Johnston fired three more shots to the northeast across the busy thoroughfare, Sgt. Yeager said.
Skid-mark evidence showed that the Jimmy was "clearly
out of control" at that point, Sgt. Yeager added.

A split second later, one of two police cruisers that had been pursuing Mr. Seguin rammed the driver's side of the vehicle, which spun onto the sidewalk and continued travelling back toward police officers stationed in the area.
Sgt. Johnston, who had by then changed positions, fired two more shots.
"I am quite confident that one of those two shots was the one that killed Mr. Seguin," Sgt. Yeager told the five-person coroner's jury.
An autopsy determined that Mr. Seguin died of a single gunshot wound to the head.

One of the three shots fired by Constable Watson hit a bus shelter, while another lodged in the fender of a red Yaris owned by Victoria resident Francois Blouin, who pulled over when he saw the police emergency lights.
Investigators recovered only nine of the 12 slugs that were fired that day, Sgt. Yeager said.
None of the officers on the scene knew the identity of the suspect, which was confirmed by fingerprint analysis the next day, he added.

Tim Harper, a collision analyst hired by the coroner's service, testified that police rammed Mr. Seguin's vehicle "at least three times" as they tried to disable the Jimmy just before the brief police pursuit.
Two police cruisers that had placed the stolen Jimmy under surveillance earlier in the evening moved in as soon as Mr. Seguin got behind the wheel.
Mr. Seguin hit one of the vehicles head-on as he tried to drive away. A second police car then hit the Jimmy from behind as it was accelerating in reverse.
The Jimmy jumped the curb, hit the side of a tree and spun around as the first cruiser rammed it again, bending the driver's side front wheel outward at a 45-degree angle.
Barely under control, the Jimmy shot across Quadra Street and came to rest against a rock wall. But police were unable to pin the vehicle and Mr. Seguin sped away with two squad cars in hot pursuit.
The inquest wraps up today at the Victoria court house.
Special to The Globe and Mail
